claims.text: Oxidation resistance in high-temperature MPEAs is governed by the ability to form a continuous Cr-rich oxide scale.
A continuous Cr-rich oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier.
MPEAs with sufficient Cr form a protective oxide scale more readily.
Elements synergistic with Cr may promote the stability of the protective Cr-rich oxide.
Formation of the protective Cr-rich scale produces slower oxidation kinetics and enhanced material integrity.
Increasing alloy Cr concentration at elevated temperature leads to preferential oxidation of Cr.
Preferential Cr oxidation forms a continuous, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
The Cr-rich oxide layer impedes oxygen diffusion into the alloy bulk.
Impeded oxygen diffusion reduces degradation of the alloy.
The higher-Cr alloy will have a lower oxidation rate than the lower-Cr baseline.
The higher-Cr alloy will show less weight gain per unit area than the lower-Cr baseline.
The higher-Cr alloy will form a thinner oxide scale than the lower-Cr baseline.
The higher-Cr alloy's oxide scale will be continuous, adherent, and Cr-rich.
The lower-Cr baseline will form a less protective scale and consequently exhibit greater oxidation and oxide-scale thickness.
The proposed governing behavior applies where oxidation kinetics are controlled by scale formation and Cr availability limits protective-scale formation.
Scale spallation or volatilization at extreme temperatures may cause departures from the proposed behavior.
Protective Cr-rich scale formation is well documented in simple alloys.
Additional phases or competitive oxidation pathways in MPEAs may alter the effectiveness of Cr-rich scale formation.
The critical Cr concentration and its interactions with other alloying elements are not specified and remain uncertain.
A controlled comparison can test the hypothesis by exposing higher- and lower-Cr MPEAs to identical oxidation conditions and comparing mass gain, scale thickness, continuity, and composition.
